title: Fixed & Recurring Deposits (FDs and RDs)
tagline: The safest, most familiar Indian instruments. Guaranteed returns, fully predictable — and quietly eroded by tax and inflation. When they're the right tool, and when they're a trap for long-term money.
summary: How FDs and RDs work, their guaranteed-but-modest returns, taxation, and their real role.

items.detail: You lock a lump sum with a bank for a chosen term (7 days to 10 years) at a fixed interest rate agreed up front. You get the principal plus interest at maturity. Breaking early usually costs a small penalty.
Same idea, but you deposit a fixed amount every month for a fixed term — ideal when you don't have a lump sum but can save monthly. It's the 'SIP' of the safe-deposit world.

blocks.title: The safety net
blocks.text: Bank deposits (FD + RD + savings) are insured by DICGC up to ₹5 lakh per bank per depositor. The returns are also contractually guaranteed — you know the exact maturity value on day one. This certainty is their entire appeal.

paragraphs: FD/RD interest is **fully taxable at your income-tax slab rate** and added to your income each year (banks deduct TDS once interest crosses a threshold). For someone in the 30% slab, a 7% FD becomes about **4.9% after tax**.

Now subtract inflation (~6%). A post-tax 4.9% return against 6% inflation is a **negative real return** — the money grows on paper but loses buying power. This is the core reason FDs are wrong for long-term wealth: they're safe in rupees but unsafe in *purchasing power*.

blocks.title: Real return, worked
blocks.result: ≈ 4.9% − 6% = **about −1.1% real**. For Aarav, who currently pays no tax (income below the limit), the post-tax return is the full ~7%, so his real return is roughly flat — still not wealth-building, but not losing either.

blocks.text: Note how the same FD is worse for a high earner (30% slab) than for Aarav (no tax). Taxation changes which asset is 'best' depending on your slab — a theme we'll return to in Module 6.

sections.title: When FDs/RDs are the right tool

blocks.title: FD / RD honestly
pros: Money you'll need within 1–3 years (capital protection matters more than growth)
Part of an emergency fund (sweep-in FDs especially)
The 'safe' portion of a goal as its deadline approaches
Anyone who truly cannot tolerate any volatility
cons: Long-term wealth building (15–30 years) — inflation and tax win
Goals where you have time to ride out equity volatility
Beating inflation meaningfully — they're not designed to

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: FDs/RDs are a capital-PROTECTION tool, not a wealth-CREATION tool. Use them for short-horizon, can't-lose-it money. For long-term goals, their guaranteed safety is exactly what makes them lose to inflation.

cheatsheet: FD = lock a lump sum at a fixed rate; RD = deposit a fixed amount monthly. Returns are guaranteed.
Bank deposits insured by DICGC up to ₹5 lakh per bank per depositor.
Interest is fully taxable at your slab; a 7% FD ≈ 4.9% post-tax in the 30% slab.
Post-tax FD often trails ~6% inflation → negative real return for high earners.
Right for short-term (1–3 yr) or can't-lose money; wrong for long-term wealth.
Capital-protection tool, not a wealth-creation tool.

questions.prompt: Aarav's uncle (30% tax slab) says 'FDs at 7% are great, totally safe, I'll never touch equity.' What's the hidden problem with this for his long-term retirement money?
questions.hint: Compute the return after tax, then after inflation.
answer: A 7% FD in the 30% slab returns only ~4.9% after tax. Against ~6% inflation, that's roughly **−1.1% in real terms** — his retirement money is slowly *losing* buying power every year despite the balance rising. 'Totally safe' in rupees is quietly unsafe in purchasing power.

For multi-decade money, the uncle needs assets that beat inflation after tax (e.g. equity/index funds). FDs are perfect for short-term and emergency money, but using them for long-term wealth guarantees he falls behind.
keyPoints: Safe in rupees, unsafe in buying power

questions.prompt: Aarav wants to save for a laptop he'll buy in 14 months. Should he use an RD or an equity SIP? Why?
questions.hint: How much time is there to recover from a market dip?
answer: An **RD** (or short FD). With only ~14 months, there isn't enough time to ride out an equity downturn — if the market falls 20% right before he buys, his goal is wrecked. An RD gives a guaranteed maturity value he can plan around, which is exactly what a short, fixed-deadline goal needs.

This is goal-and-timeline matching (Module 5): short horizon → capital protection → debt-style instruments; long horizon → growth → equity. The RD's modest return is a fair price for certainty over 14 months.
keyPoints: No time to recover from an equity dip
